His research concerned polymer synthesis and applications, particularly polyurethane chemistry, elastomers, synthetic rubber, reactive oligomers, polymer compositions, adhesives, sealants, coatings, and rubber recycling. He spent most of his Soviet scientific career at the All-Union Research Institute of Synthetic Rubber named after Academician S. V. Lebedev (VNIISK) in Leningrad. His Soviet inventive activity is documented from 1966 through 1990, and after emigrating to the United States in 1990 he continued work in polymer chemistry and industrial research. Early life and education Rappoport was born on 26 November 1935. According to family and biographical information, he was born in Leningrad, Soviet Union. He studied at the Leningrad Forestry Institute, later incorporated into the institution now known as Saint Petersburg State Forest Technical University named after S. M. Kirov. Scientific career in the Soviet Union Rappoport’s professional scientific career was associated with VNIISK in Leningrad, a major Soviet research organization concerned with synthetic rubber, latex, rubber compounds, and polymer technology. I. V. Garmonov’s history of Soviet synthetic-rubber science identifies Rappoport among the principal participants in work that led to pilot-industrial production of urethane rubbers at a Kazan plant in 1967. In 1972 an exploratory research group was established under his direction; its principal objective was the synthesis of non-isocyanate urethane elastomers. In 1983 a laboratory was established under his leadership for the rational utilization of rubber waste, particularly polyisoprene. Doctor of Chemical Sciences In 1983 Rappoport defended the doctoral dissertation Новые уретансодержащие эластомеры и реакционноспособные олигомеры (синтез, свойства, применение) (New urethane-containing elastomers and reactive oligomers: synthesis, properties and applications). The work was associated with the Institute of Chemical Physics of the Academy of Sciences of the USSR. He received the Soviet degree Doctor of Chemical Sciences (доктор химических наук). Research and inventions Rappoport’s Soviet patent record documents inventive activity from at least 1966 through 1990. His earliest verified filing is SU 223335, a method for producing copolymers of propylene oxide, filed in 1966. SU 287292, an epoxy composition, was filed on 6 June 1969. During the 1970s and 1980s his inventions covered synthetic rubber, vulcanization, polyurethane and urethane chemistry, cast elastomers, epoxy and thermoplastic compositions, adhesives, sealants, multilayer materials, reactive compounds, coatings, and rubber reclamation. The breadth of the record indicates a broad polymer-chemistry program with particular strength in urethane/polyurethane and elastomer technology. Scientific publications Rappoport co-authored publications on catalytic degradation of polyurethanes, urethane-containing glycols, polyurethane isocyanurates, polyacetalurethanes, and polyurethane elastomers. A 1981 publication concerned polyurethane elastomers produced without diisocyanates, corresponding closely to the non-isocyanate polyurethane research documented in the VNIISK history. Career in the United States Rappoport emigrated to the United States in 1990 and continued his work in polymer chemistry. US 5,175,231, Urethane oligomers and polyurethanes, was granted in 1992 to Leonid Rappoport and Roger D. Brown. He later became associated with Polymeright, Inc., and was named on U.S. patents concerning urethane- and urea-containing oligomers, epoxy-amine systems, ebonite coatings, protective coatings, and sulfur-containing polymers. Industrial and defense-related research In 2004 Rappoport was principal investigator for a U.S. Department of Defense Small Business Innovation Research project entitled Fast Cure Primer and Non-Skid System and/or a Single Coat Non-Skid System. title: Draft:Run Army
creator: LukeMoloney
disclosure: <!-- Do not remove this line! --> {{AfC comment|1=In preparing this draft, I disclose that AI assistance was used as follows: {{Hidden begin}}nowiki'''Run Army''' is an Australian community running event associated with the [[Australian Army]]. The event was established in [[Brisbane]], Queensland, in 2021 and has subsequently expanded to include events in other Australian locations and virtual participation. Run Army combines running and walking events with community engagement, fundraising and participation by Australian Defence Force personnel, veterans, emergency services personnel and members of the public. The event was originally established as a fundraiser for [[Legacy Australia|Legacy]], an Australian organisation supporting the families of veterans who have died or become incapacitated. Its fundraising activities have subsequently expanded to include organisations supporting veterans, police, ambulance, fire and emergency-service personnel, surf lifesavers and other community organisations. == History == === Establishment === The inaugural Run Army was held at [[Gallipoli Barracks]] in [[Enoggera, Queensland|Enoggera]], Brisbane, in April 2021. More than 1,000 soldiers and civilians participated in 5-kilometre and 10-kilometre events, raising more than A$46,000 for Legacy.<ref>{{cite web |title=Running for Legacy |url=https://www.defence.gov.au/news-events/news/2021-04-21/running-legacy |website=Defence |date=21 April 2021 |access-date=9 October 2026}}</ref> The event formed part of the Australian Army's broader physical fitness, wellbeing and community engagement activities. It was associated with an eight-week Army running program intended to improve physical fitness and endurance among participants.<ref>{{cite web |title=Army opens Brisbane Barracks for inaugural Run Army charity run |url=https://www.minister.defence.gov.au/media-releases/2021-04-18/army-opens-brisbane-barracks-inaugural-run-army-charity-run |website=Australian Government Department of Defence |date=18 April 2021 |access-date=9 October 2026}}</ref> === Expansion to Brisbane's central business district === The 2022 event was moved from Gallipoli Barracks to central Brisbane. Approximately 3,500 people participated in person, with more than 1,000 additional virtual participants. More than A$150,000 was raised for Legacy.<ref>{{cite web |title=Fun Run raises more than $150,000 for Legacy |url=https://www.defence.gov.au/news-events/news/2022-05-02/fun-run-raises-more-than-150000-legacy |website=Defence |date=2 May 2022 |access-date=9 October 2026}}</ref> The move into central Brisbane involved cooperation between the Australian Army, Queensland Police Service, Queensland Government and Brisbane City Council.<ref>{{cite web |title=Fun Run raises more than $150,000 for Legacy |url=https://www.defence.gov.au/news-events/news/2022-05-02/fun-run-raises-more-than-150000-legacy |website=Defence |date=2 May 2022 |access-date=9 October 2026}}</ref> === Expansion and satellite events === The 2023 Run Army program attracted more than 9,500 participants across Australia and internationally. The Brisbane event attracted more than 5,000 participants, while satellite events were held in locations including Townsville, Darwin and the Pilbara, as well as overseas locations including Port Moresby and Texas. More than A$215,000 was raised for Legacy.<ref>{{cite web |title=Army's runaway success |url=https://www.defence.gov.au/news-events/news/2023-05-08/armys-runaway-success |website=Defence |date=8 May 2023 |access-date=9 October 2026}}</ref> A Run Army event was established in [[Townsville]] in 2023. The event was held at [[Jezzine Barracks]] and attracted Australian Defence Force personnel and members of the local community, with proceeds supporting Northern Queensland Legacy.<ref>{{cite web |title=Running for a purpose |url=https://www.defence.gov.au/news-events/news/2023-04-27/running-purpose |website=Defence |date=27 April 2023 |access-date=9 October 2026}}</ref> === First responder partnerships === From 2024, Run Army expanded its community and fundraising partnerships to include emergency service organisations. Queensland Police Service, Queensland Ambulance Service and Queensland Fire and Emergency Services personnel participated alongside Australian Army personnel and members of the public.<ref>{{cite web |title=Time to get ready for Run Army |url=https://www.defence.gov.au/news-events/news/2024-03-14/time-get-ready-run-army |website=Defence |date=14 March 2024 |access-date=9 October 2026}}</ref> The 2024 Brisbane event attracted approximately 6,500 participants. Including satellite and virtual events elsewhere in Australia and overseas, participation exceeded 10,000.<ref>{{cite web |title=Run Army goes global |url=https://www.defence.gov.au/news-events/news/2024-04-24/run-army-goes-global |website=Defence |date=24 April 2024 |access-date=9 October 2026}}</ref> The Townsville event attracted more than 2,400 participants in 2024. The event included military personnel, emergency service personnel and members of the public, with fundraising supporting organisations associated with veterans and emergency services.<ref>{{cite news |title=Support shines through at Run Army 2024 |url=https://www.couriermail.com.au/news/run-army-2024-a-hit-as-thousands-turn-out-to-support-townsvilles-troops-and-services/news-story/20dbbb6e19d25909c2e8d12526fa8bf9 |work=The Courier-Mail |date=21 April 2024 |access-date=9 October 2026}}</ref> === 2025 === The 2025 Brisbane event attracted 7,651 entrants. The event continued to expand its partnerships with organisations representing veterans and emergency services, with fundraising involving Legacy, Queensland Police Legacy, the Queensland Ambulance Service Legacy Scheme, the Firefighters Cancer Foundation and other community organisations.<ref>{{cite web |title=Run Army participants dig deep for Legacy |url=https://www.defence.gov.au/news-events/news/2025-04-14/run-army-participants-dig-deep-legacy |website=Defence |date=14 April 2025 |access-date=9 October 2026}}</ref> The 2025 event also involved the Queensland State Emergency Service and Surf Life Saving organisations. RSL Queensland continued its role as a major partner of the event.<ref>{{cite web |title=Run Army 2025 Event Guide |url=https://runarmy.org.au/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/RAB25-Event-Guide-Working-Draft.pdf |website=Run Army |date=2025 |access-date=9 October 2026}}</ref> === 2026 === The 2026 Brisbane event attracted more than 10,000 entrants, making it the largest Brisbane Run Army event to that point. It was the sixth iteration of the event.<ref>{{cite web |title=Crowds converge on Brisbane for Run Army |url=https://www.defence.gov.au/news-events/news/2026-04-07/crowds-converge-brisbane-run-army |website=Defence |date=7 April 2026 |access-date=9 October 2026}}</ref> The 2026 Brisbane program included 5-kilometre and 10-kilometre events, a 2.4-kilometre junior event and a 15-kilometre Chiefs Challenge.<ref>{{cite web |title=Crowds converge on Brisbane for Run Army |url=https://www.defence.gov.au/news-events/news/2026-04-07/crowds-converge-brisbane-run-army |website=Defence |date=7 April 2026 |access-date=9 October 2026}}</ref> By 2026, more than 30,000 people had participated in Run Army events since the event's establishment.<ref>{{cite web |title=Crowds converge on Brisbane for Run Army |url=https://www.defence.gov.au/news-events/news/2026-04-07/crowds-converge-brisbane-run-army |website=Defence |date=7 April 2026 |access-date=9 October 2026}}</ref> A 2026 reception hosted by the [[Governor of Queensland]] reported that Run Army had raised nearly A$850,000 since 2021. The event's beneficiaries included Legacy, Queensland Police Legacy, the Firefighters Cancer Foundation, the Queensland Ambulance Service Legacy Scheme, the Queensland State Emergency Service Gift Fund, Surf Life Saving Foundation and the Indigenous Marathon Foundation.<ref>{{cite web |title=Reception in support of Run Army 2026 |url=https://www.govhouse.qld.gov.au/the-governor-of-queensland/speeches/reception-in-support-of-run-army-2026 |website=Government House Queensland |date=2026 |access-date=9 October 2026}}</ref> == Events and locations == Run Army's principal events have been held in Brisbane and Townsville, with additional satellite events and virtual participation in other locations. The Brisbane event has generally been held in the South Bank and central Brisbane areas. The course has incorporated sections of Brisbane's central business district and surrounding areas, including crossings of the [[Brisbane River]] and routes near major city landmarks.<ref>{{cite web |title=Run Army 2025 |url=https://www.army.gov.au/news-and-events/events/2025-03-30/run-army-2025 |website=Australian Army |date=30 March 2025 |access-date=9 October 2026}}</ref> The Townsville event has been based around the [[Strand, Townsville|Strand]] and Jezzine Barracks.<ref>{{cite web |title=Running for a purpose |url=https://www.defence.gov.au/news-events/news/2023-04-27/running-purpose |website=Defence |date=27 April 2023 |access-date=9 October 2026}}</ref> Satellite and virtual events have enabled Australian Defence Force personnel and members of the public to participate outside the principal host cities. In 2024, Run Army reported participation from Australia and overseas locations.<ref>{{cite web |title=Run Army goes global |url=https://www.defence.gov.au/news-events/news/2024-04-24/run-army-goes-global |website=Defence |date=24 April 2024 |access-date=9 October 2026}}</ref> == Race format == Run Army's principal races have traditionally consisted of 5-kilometre and 10-kilometre distances. Participants may run or walk the shorter event. The Brisbane program was expanded in 2026 to include a 2.4-kilometre junior event and a 15-kilometre Chiefs Challenge.<ref>{{cite web |title=Crowds converge on Brisbane for Run Army |url=https://www.defence.gov.au/news-events/news/2026-04-07/crowds-converge-brisbane-run-army |website=Defence |date=7 April 2026 |access-date=9 October 2026}}</ref> The event has also included participation by Australian Defence Force and emergency-service personnel and displays of Defence equipment and capabilities.<ref>{{cite web |title=Run Army goes global |url=https://www.defence.gov.au/news-events/news/2024-04-24/run-army-goes-global |website=Defence |date=24 April 2024 |access-date=9 October 2026}}</ref> == Winners and records == Run Army awards overall winners and podium places in its principal competitive events. She served as chair of the Bergen-Belsen Survivors Organization in Israel from January 2022 until her death in February 2024. She was the first woman, and the first person born in the Bergen-Belsen displaced persons camp, to chair the organization. She was also editor-in-chief of the organization's international journal, ''Our Voice''.<ref name="bergen2022">{{cite web |url=https://bergenbelsen.org/2022/01/02/%D7%94%D7%99%D7%A1%D7%98%D7%95%D7%A8%D7%99%D7%94-%D7%91%D7%90%D7%A8%D7%92%D7%95%D7%9F-%D7%91%D7%9C%D7%96%D7%9F-%D7%91%D7%99%D7%A9%D7%A8%D7%90%D7%9C-%D7%99%D7%95%D7%9B%D7%99-%D7%A8%D7%99%D7%A5-%D7%99/ |title=History in the Belsen organization in Israel: Jochi Ritz-Olewski, born in Bergen-Belsen, elected chairperson of the organization |website=Bergen-Belsen Survivors Organization in Israel |date=2 January 2022 |access-date=15 October 2026}}</ref> == Early life == Ritz-Olewski was born Jocheved-Rivka Olewski on 15 March 1947 at the Glyn Hughes Hospital in the [[Bergen-Belsen displaced persons camp]] in Germany.<ref name="mynet2024">{{cite news |last=Atadgi |first=Asher |title=שורדת השואה האהובה והפעילה החברתית יוכי ריץ-אולבסקי הלכה לעולמה |url=https://raanana.mynet.co.il/local_news/article/h1oyduenp |work=mynet Ra'anana |date=19 February 2024 |language=he |access-date=15 October 2026}}</ref><ref name="JA2010">{{cite news |last=Trojanowski |first=Martina |title=Babyboom in Bergen-Belsen |url=https://www.juedische-allgemeine.de/politik/babyboom-in-bergen-belsen/ |work=Jüdische Allgemeine |date=12 April 2010 |language=de |access-date=15 October 2026}}</ref> Her parents, Rachela Zelmanowicz-Olewski and Rafael Gershon Olewski, were Holocaust survivors. Her mother had been imprisoned at [[Auschwitz concentration camp|Auschwitz]], where she played the mandolin in the [[Women's Orchestra of Auschwitz]]. Her father survived [[Monowitz concentration camp|Auschwitz III–Monowitz (Buna)]] and Bergen-Belsen and later became a journalist, writer and one of the founders and chairmen of the Bergen-Belsen Survivors Organization in Israel.<ref name="bergen2022" /> Her parents met after liberation and married in [[Celle]], Germany, in 1946.<ref name="JA2010" /> In April 1949 the family immigrated to Israel. They initially lived in [[Bnei Brak]] and later moved to [[Ramat Gan]].<ref name="mynet2024" /> She served in an intelligence unit of the [[Israel Defense Forces]], where she acquired the nickname "Jochi".<ref name="mynet2024" /> == Education and career == Ritz-Olewski studied at the [[Hebrew University of Jerusalem]], earning a bachelor's degree in English and French as well as a teaching certificate. She later earned a master's degree with distinction in public administration from [[Bar-Ilan University]].<ref name="mynet2024" /> Early in her career, she worked at the [[Technion – Israel Institute of Technology]], where she coordinated a pre-academic preparatory program.<ref name="mynet2024" /> In 1978 she joined the [[Open University of Israel]]. During her career there she held administrative positions in the Dean of Academic Studies' office and served for many years as deputy dean of academic studies.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.openu.ac.il/Lists/MediaServer_Documents/about/Departments/president_report/2008/06-09.pdf |title=University authorities |publisher=Open University of Israel |date=2008 |language=he |access-date=15 October 2026}}</ref><ref name="mynet2019">{{cite news |last=Kimeron |first=Benny |title=סוגרת מעגל: תושבת רעננה שנולדה בברגן בבלזן חנכה השבוע במקום מרכז הנצחה |url=https://raanana.mynet.co.il/local_news/article/m_380468 |work=mynet Ra'anana |date=1 May 2019 |language=he |access-date=15 October 2026}}</ref> She retired from the Open University in 2014.<ref name="bergen2022" /> == Holocaust remembrance and Bergen-Belsen activities == Alongside her professional career, Ritz-Olewski was active in the Bergen-Belsen Survivors Organization in Israel. She joined its leadership after people born in the displaced persons camp and members of subsequent generations became involved in the organization, and later served as deputy chair.<ref name="mynet2019" /> She represented the Israeli organization in the international advisory framework associated with the Lower Saxony Memorials Foundation in Germany.<ref name="bergen2022" /> In 2012 Ritz-Olewski signed a declaration calling for the preservation of the former Bergen-Belsen displaced persons camp area, historically significant buildings and the Jewish cemetery, and for their incorporation into the Bergen-Belsen memorial landscape.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bergen-belsen.de/fileadmin/Webshop/E-Book/Jahresbericht_SnG_2012.pdf |title=Jahresbericht 2012 |publisher=Stiftung niedersächsische Gedenkstätten |date=2012 |language=de |access-date=15 October 2026}}</ref> In 2019 she participated in efforts that led to the transfer of five historic buildings in the former displaced persons camp area to the Lower Saxony Memorials Foundation for preservation and educational use.<ref name="mynet2019" /> That year she was also involved in the organization's campaign against the auction of a historic Bergen-Belsen rabbinical court ledger, arguing that documents of Holocaust-era historical significance should remain accessible to the public.<ref>{{cite news |last=Sharon |first=Jeremy |title=Bergen-Belsen survivors petition court to halt sale of camp ledger |url=https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/bergen-belsen-survivors-petitions-court-to-halt-sale-of-ledger-from-concentration-camp-609652 |work=The Jerusalem Post |date=3 December 2019 |access-date=15 October 2026}}</ref> == ''Our Voice'' == Ritz-Olewski and her brother Arie Olewski revived ''Our Voice'', the journal of the Bergen-Belsen Survivors Organization in Israel. The publication continued the tradition of the Yiddish newspaper ''Unzer Sztyme'', which had been published in the Bergen-Belsen displaced persons camp after the Second World War and with which their father Rafael Olewski had been involved.<ref name="mynet2019" /> Ritz-Olewski served as editor-in-chief of ''Our Voice'', which covered Bergen-Belsen survivors, the displaced persons camp, later generations and the preservation of the community's historical memory.<ref name="bergen2022" /> == Chair of the Bergen-Belsen Survivors Organization in Israel == Ritz-Olewski was elected chair of the Bergen-Belsen Survivors Organization in Israel and began serving on 1 January 2022, succeeding [[Shraga Milstein]].<ref name="bergen2022" /> She remained chair until her death in February 2024. In March 2024 her brother, Arie Olewski, was elected chair of the organization.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://bergenbelsen.org/2024/03/23/%D7%90%D7%A8%D7%99%D7%94-%D7%90%D7%95%D7%9C%D7%91%D7%A1%D7%A7%D7%99-%D7%A0%D7%91%D7%97%D7%A8-%D7%9C%D7%99%D7%95%D7%A8-%D7%94%D7%97%D7%93%D7%A9-%D7%A9%D7%9C-%D7%94%D7%90%D7%A8%D7%92%D7%95%D7%9F-arie/ |title=Arie Olewski is the new Chairman |website=Bergen-Belsen Survivors Organization in Israel |date=23 March 2024 |access-date=15 October 2026}}</ref> == Personal life == Ritz-Olewski married Oded Ritz in 1969. [[George Nathaniel Curzon]] had identified what became known as Curzon’s Ice Cave as the source in 1895.<ref name="Colegrave2012">{{cite journal |last=Colegrave |first=Bill |title=Half-Way to Heaven: Research on the Source of the Oxus River |journal=Asian Affairs |volume=43 |issue=1 |pages=27–48 |year=2012 |doi=10.1080/03068374.2012.643599 }}</ref><ref name="McCowan2026" /> The expedition reached the Ice Cave and then investigated the other three claimed headwaters of the river that had been considered competitors to the Ice Cave. It found a stream called the Chelab Stream and discovered that it bifurcates and feeds both sides of the Little Pamir watershed and is the common source of two of the three. The Chelab could therefore be regarded as the source or parent stream of the Amu Darya (Oxus).<ref name="Ibbotson2026" /><ref name="McCowan2026" /><ref name="Chan2011">{{cite news |last=Chan |first=Joyee |title=In search of the Oxus |url=https://www.scmp.com/article/984882/search-oxus |work=South China Morning Post |date=16 November 2011 |access-date=13 November 2026 }}</ref> Colegrave described the expedition in ''Halfway House to Heaven: Unravelling the Mystery of the Majestic River Oxus'', published by Bene Factum in 2010.<ref name="HalfwayHouse">{{cite book |last=Colegrave |first=Bill |title=Halfway House to Heaven: Unravelling the Mystery of the Majestic River Oxus |publisher=Bene Factum |year=2010 }}</ref> He subsequently published his research in ''Asian Affairs''.<ref name="Colegrave2012" /> Two separate expeditions attempted to trace the source of the Chelab itself in 2025. Their differing findings were published in volume 57, issue 1 of ''Asian Affairs''.<ref name="Ibbotson2026" /><ref name="McCowan2026" /> Colegrave undertook a follow-up journey in 2026 from [[Ishkashim]] at the western end of the Wakhan Corridor around [[Badakhshan]].<ref name="Oldie2026">{{cite web |last=Colegrave |first=Bill |title=Through the Pamirs |url=https://www.theoldie.co.uk/blog/through-the-pamirs-by-bill-colgrave |website=The Oldie |date=7 July 2026 |access-date=13 November 2026 }}</ref> Colegrave also compiled ''Scraps of Wool: A Journey Through the Golden Age of Travel Writing'', a collection of travel writing published by Unbound in 2017.<ref name="Penguin" /> ==Political activity== At the [[2024 United Kingdom general election]], Colegrave stood as the Rejoin EU candidate for [[Hammersmith and Chiswick (UK Parliament constituency)|Hammersmith and Chiswick]]. He received 821 votes, representing 1.8 per cent of the vote.<ref name="Parliament2024">{{cite web |title=Election result for Hammersmith and Chiswick |url=https://members.parliament.uk/constituency/4079/election/422 |website=UK Parliament |date=4 July 2024 |access-date=13 November 2026 }}</ref> This was the highest vote total and percentage received by any Rejoin EU candidate in the election.<ref name="RejoinResults">{{cite web |title=General Election 2024 results |url=https://therejoineuparty.com/rejoin-eu-party-general-election-2024-results/ |website=The Rejoin EU Party |publisher=The Rejoin EU Party |access-date=13 November 2026 }}</ref> ==Sport== Colegrave and David Jenkins won the United States over-55s doubles [[real tennis]] championship in 2005.<ref name="USCTA">{{cite web |title=Record of Champions |url=https://uscourttennis.org/record-of-champions-toggle/ |website=United States Court Tennis Association |access-date=13 November 2026 }}</ref> Colegrave also represented Great Britain at senior level in real tennis and at the World [[Pétanque]] Championships.<ref name="Penguin" /> ==References== {{reflist}}</nowiki>{{hidden end}} <!--Comment automatically added by the Submission Wizard-->

A professional racing driver by profession and the first Malaysian from the State of Sarawak to compete in GT cars and LMP3, racing between 2009 and 2021. Over the course of Zen’s career, he has entered 136 races, securing 58 podium finishes and 20 victories before retiring. Born in the State of Kuching to a working-class family, Zen Low began kart racing competitively at the age of 18. However, due to financial limitations, it forced him to stop his kart racing after just one season. In 1995, he began jet ski racing with Team Wong Way Racing, where he became champion in the Novice Runabout Open category of the Malaysian Jet Sports Championship. The following year, he joined Team Petronas Jetsport, achieving 10 podium finishes, out of which six were in the number one spot, and finishing second overall in the championship. By 1998, financial constraints once again brought his racing ambition to a halt. In 2009, Zen Low, still burning with determination and drive in motorsports, transitioned to car racing after securing sufficient funding. He began his GT career with Lotus Cars Malaysia, driving a Lotus Elise Mk1 in the Malaysia Merdeka Endurance Race (MMER) 12 Hours, where he qualified second but luck was not on his side as he did not finish the race due to technical issue. In 2010, Zen competed in the Megalap Time Attack, finishing second in the Supersport Production class, and won the European Car category in the Zerotohundred Time Attack. That same year, he returned to Malaysia Merdeka Endurance Race (MMER) with a Lotus 2-Eleven, this time again qualifying second but retired from the race. In 2011, Zen took part in the Malaysia Super Series race, finishing second overall in a Lotus Exige. But in the MMER 12 Hours race, he qualified second but fate has it that he again did not finish the race. The following year, in 2012, he finally broke the chain of bad fortune and claimed the national championship title in the Malaysia Super Series with seven podium finishes. His success continued in 2013 when he won the Asian Le Mans Series (3 Hours of Sepang) in the GTC category with a Lamborghini Gallardo GT3. He also finished second overall in the Lamborghini Blancpain Super Trofeo Asia Pacific with five podiums and secured second place in the GT4 class at the MMER 12 Hours with a Lotus Evora. In 2014, he was placed third overall in the Lamborghini Blancpain Super Trofeo Asia Pacific, having seven podium finishes. In 2015, Zen finished second overall in the CN class of the Asian Le Mans Series driving a Wolf prototype. He was placed seventh overall in the GT Asia Series driving a Lamborghini Gallardo GT3, and finished seventh overall in the Sepang 12 Hours endurance race with a Lamborghini Huracán GT3. 2016 was a good year for Zen Low. He got second and third position in the Sprint Cup of the Asian Le Mans Series, seventh overall in the Endurance Cup with an LMP3 Ginetta, second overall with eight podiums in the Lamborghini Blancpain Super Trofeo Asia and was crowned the overall GT4 champion for the Sepang 12 Hours with a Ginetta. In 2017, Zen became the first and only Malaysian to be fully sponsored by Ferrari Malaysia to compete in the Ferrari Challenge Asia-Pacific, where he finished third overall with seven podiums. That same year, he competed in the Bathurst 12 Hour endurance race, finishing fourth in the GT4 category. In 2018, he was selected by the Motorsport Association of Malaysia (MAM) to represent the country at the inaugural FIA GT Nations Cup in Bahrain. Team Malaysia finished eighth overall with an Audi R8 GT3. In 2019, Zen secured third overall in the Lamborghini Super Trofeo Asia Pacific championship with seven podium finishes. After the disruption by the COVID-19 pandemic, Zen concluded his racing career in 2021 on a high note by winning the Sepang 1000 km Endurance Race in the Toyota Vios Enduro Cup. From 2022 to 2026, Zen Low has remained active in motorsport as a drifting driver, collaborating with International and local brands such as Monster Energy, Goodyear, Autobacs, Milwaukee, TikTok Malaysia, XPEL, and Carlist. Family Zen Low was born on 12 February 1969 in Kuching, Sarawak, East Malaysia, into a working-class family. His father, Low Ngi Huat, was a businessman in the entertainment industry, while his mother, Then Moi Ing, was a homemaker who also assisted in the family business. He is one of four siblings, with two sisters and one brother. [[User:Kisseran|Kisseran]] ([[User talk:Kisseran|talk]]) 17:14, 10 November 2026 (UTC)}} {{AfC comment|1=In preparing this draft, I disclose that AI assistance was used as follows: {{Hidden begin}}nowiki{{LLM-assisted translation}} {{Short description|French harpsichordist and author (born 1960)}} {{Infobox musical artist | name = Olivier Baumont | background = non_vocal_instrumentalist | birth_date = {{Birth date and age|1960|8|15|df=yes}} | birth_place = [[Saint-Dié-des-Vosges]], France | instrument = [[Harpsichord]] | occupation = Harpsichordist, author, teacher | genre = [[Classical music]], [[Baroque music]] | website = {{URL|https://www.olivierbaumont.fr/}} }} '''Olivier Baumont''' (born 15 August 1960) is a French [[harpsichordist]], author and teacher. His career has focused particularly on French keyboard music of the 17th and 18th centuries. He has taught harpsichord at the [[Conservatoire de Paris]] since 2001 and has recorded the complete harpsichord works of [[François Couperin]], [[Jean-Philippe Rameau]] and [[Jacques Duphly]].<ref name="Larousse">{{cite encyclopedia |title=Olivier Baumont |encyclopedia=Dictionnaire de la musique |publisher=Larousse |url=https://www.larousse.fr/encyclopedie/musdico/Olivier_Baumont/166144 |language=fr }}</ref><ref name="CNSMDP">{{cite web |title=Olivier Baumont |url=https://www.conservatoiredeparis.fr/fr/enseignant/baumont-olivier |website=Conservatoire de Paris |language=fr |access-date=10 November 2026 }}</ref> == Biography == === Early life and education === Born in [[Saint-Dié-des-Vosges]], France, Baumont began studying the harpsichord at the conservatory in [[Annecy]]. He continued his studies at the [[Conservatoire de Paris]], where he obtained first prizes in harpsichord and chamber music in 1981 and 1982. He subsequently studied with [[Huguette Dreyfus]] and [[Kenneth Gilbert]], and attended interpretation classes given by [[Gustav Leonhardt]] in Cologne, Germany.<ref name="CNSMDP"/> In 1982, he won the Radio France soloists' competition and made his first recording.<ref name="Larousse"/> === Musical career === Baumont has performed in recitals and chamber music concerts throughout France and internationally. He has appeared at the Ambronay Festival, the [[Festival de La Roque-d'Anthéron]], the Radio France and Montpellier Festival and events organised by the Centre de musique baroque de Versailles. His performances have also taken him to Japan, the United States, Canada, South America and various European countries.<ref name="CNSMDP"/> In the early 1990s, he became artistic director of the Festival Couperin, originally held in [[Chaumes-en-Brie]] and subsequently in [[Champs-sur-Marne]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Festival Couperin |url=https://www.lexpress.fr/informations/festival-couperin_595850.html |work=L'Express |date=23 September 1993 |language=fr }}</ref> He has collaborated with musicians including [[Davitt Moroney]], [[Jean-Paul Fouchécourt]], [[Hugo Reyne]], [[Christophe Coin]] and [[Julien Chauvin (violinist)|Julien Chauvin]]. In March 2014, Baumont initiated a series at the [[Cité de la musique]] in Paris devoted to the complete harpsichord works of [[Johann Sebastian Bach]]. The project brought together twenty harpsichordists of different generations and featured historical instruments.<ref name="CNSMDP"/> === Teaching and music research === In September 2001, Baumont was appointed professor of harpsichord at the [[Conservatoire de Paris]], where he has also taught continuo playing.<ref name="CNSMDP"/> Alongside his teaching, he gives masterclasses and lectures on historical performance practice and the French Baroque repertoire. His research has included editing and restoring keyboard music by composers such as [[Michel Corrette]], [[Jacques Duphly]] and Francis Thomé. He has also appeared on radio and television programmes devoted to classical music, including broadcasts on [[France Musique]], [[France Culture]], the BBC and Mezzo. === Theatre and cinema === Baumont's work has extended beyond the concert stage to theatre, literature and cinema. He adapted [[Denis Diderot]]'s ''[[Rameau's Nephew]]'' for the theatre. The production was performed in Paris, notably at the Théâtre Le Ranelagh, with actors Nicolas Vaude and Nicolas Marié, before touring. In 2016, he contributed the music for ''[[A Woman's Life (film)|A Woman's Life]]'' (''Une vie''), directed by [[Stéphane Brizé]] and based on the novel by [[Guy de Maupassant]]. The film's music draws in part on 18th-century keyboard works, including compositions by Jacques Duphly.<ref>{{cite web |title=Une vie |url=https://diaphana.fr/film/une-vie/ |website=Diaphana Distribution |language=fr }}</ref> Baumont has also performed with the French actor [[Denis Podalydès]] in literary concerts combining readings and harpsichord music, particularly around the works of [[Marcel Proust]].<ref name="Franciscaines">{{cite web |title=Olivier Baumont |url=https://festivallitterairedeauville.fr/fr/artistes/olivier-baumont |website=Les Franciscaines |language=fr }}</ref> === Recordings === Baumont has recorded a substantial repertoire of Baroque keyboard music. His discography includes the complete harpsichord works of [[Jean-Philippe Rameau]] and [[François Couperin]], as well as recordings devoted to [[Johann Sebastian Bach]], [[Henry Purcell]], [[George Frideric Handel]] and [[Georg Philipp Telemann]]. He has also recorded music by [[Jacques Champion de Chambonnières]], [[Louis-Claude Daquin]], [[Jean-François Dandrieu]] and [[Claude Balbastre]]. In 2022, he released ''Un clavecin pour Marcel Proust'', an album associated with the musical world of the French novelist, marking the centenary of Proust's death. In 2024, Plectra Music released his recording of works by [[Michel Corrette]], entitled ''Les Amants Enchantés & Other Harpsichord Pieces''. In 2026, Baumont released a complete recording of [[Jacques Duphly]]'s harpsichord works on the Plectra Music label. Recorded on historical harpsichords from the Flint Collection in the United States, the three-disc set comprises all 52 of Duphly's harpsichord pieces. The recording was reviewed by François Ekchajzer in ''[[Télérama]]'' in August 2026.<ref name="Duphly2026">{{cite magazine |last=Ekchajzer |first=François |title=Complete Works for Harpsichord : Jacques Duphly d'Olivier Baumont : notre critique |url=https://www.telerama.fr/musique/complete-works-for-harpsichord-jacques-duphly-d-olivier-baumont-notre-critique_cri-7045559.php |magazine=Télérama |date=25 August 2026 |language=fr }}</ref> === Writing and literary activities === In addition to his musical career, Baumont has published several books on French musical history, literature and the relationship between music and the arts. In 1998, he published ''Couperin, le musicien des rois'' in the [[Découvertes Gallimard]] collection. The book received the Prix des Muses that year.<ref name="CNSMDP"/> His 2007 book ''La Musique à Versailles'', published by Actes Sud in collaboration with the Palace of Versailles and the Centre de musique baroque de Versailles, received an award from the French music critics' association.<ref name="CNSMDP"/> He later published ''À l'Opéra, monsieur ! La musique dans les Mémoires de Saint-Simon'' (Gallimard, 2015) and ''Tombeau du jeune monsieur de Cinq-Mars'' (Arléa, 2021). In 2024, he published his first novel, ''D'une partition m'apparaissait un dessin'', with Bleu nuit. The novel was shortlisted for the 2025 Prix Livres & Musiques, awarded at Les Franciscaines in Deauville.<ref name="Franciscaines"/> === Residencies at Chambord === Baumont has maintained an artistic association with the [[Château de Chambord]], where he has performed concerts and undertaken several writing residencies. His first two residencies contributed to the development of ''À l'Opéra, monsieur !'' and ''Tombeau du jeune monsieur de Cinq-Mars''. In 2026, he undertook a third writing residency at Chambord to research a book on the history of music at the château, from the Renaissance to the present day.
